headline: Eleven entries, fourth place: the cat on Turducken’s tail

image.alt: A gigantic cream-faced blue-eyed fluffy cat wearing a restrained GPU vest enters the scoring hall. Tall Dries, five spiders, Chen’s two rabbits, Puget and Ivan, seven Turducken crew members and two Yorkies all look warily toward it. A damaged screen shows 4, the cat icon and xz.
image.caption: The cat enters the scoring hall. xz’s arrival at fourth place, October 29.

sections.heading: An entrance behind third place
sections.text:
Team Turducken has a cat problem.

A cream face, blue eyes and an expression of magnificent indifference have appeared just behind third place on the ARC-AGI-3 public leaderboard. At the early evening check, xz remained fourth on 52.95, a little over three points behind Turducken. The public entry counter said eleven.

That is an entrance worth a second look. Chen and Tufa still occupy the first two places; Turducken now has another contender close behind. The last dance sits just below xz, so the cat has company on both sides.

Our Early edition reported the arrival at fourth. The saved history supplies a useful correction to the impression of somebody materializing from nowhere: xz already had a recorded ARC-3 score of 28.41 in early October. Thursday brought the first observation of 52.95 in our collection, not a verified timestamp for the submission that produced it.

Eleven is the board’s entry count. It tells us nothing about the number of experiments, abandoned runs or hours behind those entries. But it gives the public result a striking calling card.

sections.heading: Read the form book
sections.text:
The account is xiaoz259 on Kaggle, displayed simply as xz. Its avatar is doing most of the public-facing work. The competition history supplies the form book.

When checked on October 29, the profile listed a Competitions Master ranked fifteenth, with one gold medal, three silvers and five bronzes. The gold came from first place among 4,186 teams in AI Agent Security – Multi-Step Tool Attacks.

There are silver finishes in Jane Street’s market-data forecasting contest, the second AI Mathematical Olympiad Progress Prize and NFL Big Data Bowl prediction. Earlier ARC campaigns are there too: 341st in 2024 and 602nd in 2025. Those are different contests, with different fields and tests, but they establish that this is an experienced competitor returning to ARC.

The profile directly links to GitHub account xz259, where an agent-security solution and a model reverse-engineering project are public. The reviewed self-linked profiles establish no real name, gender or nationality. For now, the name on the work is xz.

The personal biography is thin. The competitive résumé has substance.

sections.heading: Go straight to the winner
sections.text:
There is a first-place solution sitting behind that cat avatar. xz published it on September 2 after winning AI Agent Security – Multi-Step Tool Attacks. For the technical story, go straight to the winner: the full write-up and public reference code are linked below.

The ARC agent behind this fourth-place arrival still has its own story to tell.

sections.heading: The same troubled scoring hall
sections.text:
Fourth place has not insulated xz from the submission troubles occupying the rest of the paddock.

In a thread begun October 25, xz reports server startup taking anywhere from ten minutes to an hour, with slower-starting instances also appearing to deliver lower throughput. Earlier mounting trouble, the post says, was resolved. The remaining cause is unclear.

On Thursday, xz was comparing notes with other competitors about whether conditions had returned to normal. One practical detail: starting games at the ten-minute mark, then periodically sending RESET while waiting for the server.

Tufa’s Jeroen Cottaar described a different way of examining the lost time. His team believes roughly forty minutes are disappearing before the notebook itself starts, based on container uptime and total run duration. Yi-Chia Chen reported fluctuating scores while saying she could not separate infrastructure effects from ordinary run variation.

These are competitors’ observations, with different tests and different limits. Kaggle’s October 27 response said broader issues were under investigation and that capacity for individual investigations was constrained.

That is the revealing part of this otherwise sparse public portrait. The unfamiliar contender at the sharp end is also in the discussion, trying to work out where the time goes. A fourth-place result and uncertainty about run conditions can coexist.

sections.heading: The next entry
sections.text:
With Monday’s deadline approaching, the immediate race is close enough to make another improvement matter. At the early evening check, Turducken’s 56.02 left xz 3.07 points behind; the last dance, on 51.51, was only 1.44 behind xz.

Those are public-board positions. The private leaderboard will decide the final placing. For the competition desk, the live question is whether xz can turn this arrival into another move before the close.

The technical questions can wait for evidence: what changed, how reliably it worked, and how much of each run was available for solving games. The profile and security write-up give us some history. The discussion gives us a competitor willing to share the frustrating parts. The ARC breakthrough itself is still to be explained.

Our illustrator has made the entrance literal: a giant cream cat in a GPU vest, fluffy tail filling the scoring hall, while the established cast looks up from its machinery. The damaged screen displays fourth place.

The public counter says eleven. The next entry has an audience.
